title: When to Hire an Executive Assistant (and When AI Is Enough)
summary: When to hire an executive assistant versus using an AI inbox: real EA salary data, what AI can handle today, and the break-even point by company stage.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


The average US executive assistant costs $64,456 a year in base salary. An AI inbox now covers the repeatable part of that job, meaning triage, first-pass drafts and follow-up tracking, so the EA hire makes sense when work needing human judgment, relationships, complex travel and sensitive coordination outgrows software. This guide has the cost data and the break-even by stage.


## What does an executive assistant actually cost?


The national average base salary for an executive assistant in the US is $64,456 a year as of mid-2026, per ZipRecruiter, with the middle range running from about $68,000 to $104,000 depending on experience and location. That's before payroll tax, benefits, and equipment, which typically add another 20 to 30 percent to the fully-loaded cost. For an early-stage founder, that's a five- or six-figure annual commitment before the EA has answered a single email.


Most of what fills an EA's day in the first year isn't judgment work. It's triage: reading everything that comes in, drafting the replies that don't need a founder's voice, chasing threads that went quiet, and finding a meeting time that works for six calendars. That's exactly the work an AI inbox is built to absorb, which changes when the hire actually pays for itself.


## What can an AI inbox handle before you need a human?


Slashy auto-labels inbound mail into categories that match how you actually triage (Important, Calendar, Billing, and so on), drafts replies in your tone for one-click send, flags threads that went quiet with follow-up reminders, and books meetings from a calendar sidebar that sits next to the inbox rather than in a separate tab. The memory system behind all of it adapts continuously: AI-draft acceptance climbs from around 30% on day one to 80%+ by day 30 as it learns your writing style and the people you talk to most.


What it doesn't do is the work that actually requires a person: reading the room in a tense negotiation, managing a complicated multi-leg trip on the fly, or making a judgment call that depends on relationship context no software has. That's the real dividing line, not "email versus no email."


> "I was spending more time orchestrating AI than actually replying. Now I approve more than I compose. It just reads my mind."
>
>
> Michelle, Founder of The Prompting Company


## So when does the EA hire actually make sense?


When the volume of judgment work, not routine email, justifies a full-time salary. A useful test: track one week of your inbox and count how much of it is a scheduling reply, a first-pass draft, or a status update someone's waiting on. If most of it fits that description, an AI inbox covers it at a fraction of $64,000 a year, and the hire can wait until the job is actually about judgment: managing other people's calendars, handling escalations, owning projects that span outside email entirely.
